# Your own message

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 2 -->

**Needs first:** [Pick and configure the RMW](pick-the-rmw.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385.md): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.

So far the project has sent text: `std_msgs/String`, a message package that
comes with ROS 2. A sensor sends numbers, with names and units. In this
chapter you write a message package of your own, `tutorial_msgs`, with one
message, `Reading`, and change both nodes to use it. At the end the board
prints

```text
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.330477] Publishing: reading 1 (21100 mC)
[INFO] monitor_node: [    1.406537] I heard: reading 1 (21100 mC)
```

and the package you wrote is an ordinary ROS 2 message package, which a ROS
2 machine builds unchanged.

Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`.

## Write the message package

A message package is a directory under `src/` with a `package.xml`, a
`CMakeLists.txt` and one file per message. nano-ros reads the stock ROS 2
shape, so these three files are exactly what the ROS 2 documentation's
[custom interfaces tutorial](https://docs.ros.org/en/humble/Tutorials/Beginner-Client-Libraries/Custom-ROS2-Interfaces.html)
has you write. Create them in an editor, or run the commands below.

The manifest declares the package an interface package:

```bash probe=510 track=installed variant=qemu
mkdir -p src/tutorial_msgs/msg
cat > src/tutorial_msgs/package.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<package format="3">
  <name>tutorial_msgs</name>
  <version>0.1.0</version>
  <description>The Tutorial project's messages</description>
  <maintainer email="you@example.com">you</maintainer>
  <license>Apache-2.0</license>

  <buildtool_depend>ament_cmake</buildtool_depend>
  <build_depend>rosidl_default_generators</build_depend>
  <exec_depend>rosidl_default_runtime</exec_depend>
  <member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>

  <export>
    <build_type>ament_cmake</build_type>
  </export>
</package>
EOF
```

The build file asks rosidl to generate the interfaces. nano-ros never runs
this file: its build reads the package's `msg/` directory itself. It is
there so the same package builds with `colcon` on a ROS 2 machine, which
chapter 10 does.

```bash probe=515 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/tutorial_msgs/CMakeLists.txt <<'EOF'
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(tutorial_msgs)

find_package(ament_cmake REQUIRED)
find_package(rosidl_default_generators REQUIRED)

rosidl_generate_interfaces(${PROJECT_NAME}
  msg/Reading.msg
)

ament_export_dependencies(rosidl_default_runtime)
ament_package()
EOF
```

And the message, in the ROS 2 `.msg` format, one field per line:

```bash probe=520 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading.msg <<'EOF'
# One sample from the sensor node.
int32 sequence        # counts up from 1
int32 temperature_mc  # milli-degrees Celsius
EOF
```

Each line is a type and a name. The types are ROS 2's, and each maps to the
same type in every language the project can use:

| `.msg` type | Rust | C | C++ |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int32` | `i32` | `int32_t` | `int32_t` |
| `float64` | `f64` | `double` | `double` |
| `bool` | `bool` | `bool` | `bool` |
| `string` | a fixed-capacity string | a pointer, size and capacity into memory you own | a fixed-capacity string |
| `T[]` | a fixed-capacity sequence | a pointer, size and capacity into memory you own | a fixed-capacity sequence |

The last two rows are where a microcontroller shows: a string or a sequence
cannot grow at run time, because nothing allocates. What that costs is in
"What just happened" below.

Both fields are integers. The temperature is in thousandths of a degree,
`21100` for 21.1 °C, a common choice on a microcontroller: it keeps the
message small and exact, and printing it needs no floating-point formatting,
which costs flash on a board this size.

Ask `nros` whether it found the message:

```bash probe=525 track=installed variant=qemu
nros interface show tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading
```

```text
# One sample from the sensor node.
int32 sequence        # counts up from 1
int32 temperature_mc  # milli-degrees Celsius
```

`nros interface show` searches the workspace's `src/` first, then your ROS 2
install, so it prints any message a node in this workspace can use.
`nros interface list` prints all of them.

## Depend on it

Each node declares the message packages it uses in its `package.xml`.
Replace `std_msgs` with `tutorial_msgs` in both nodes:

```bash probe=530 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#<depend>std_msgs</depend>#<depend>tutorial_msgs</depend>#' \
    src/sensor_node/package.xml src/monitor_node/package.xml
```

In Rust, that is the whole change to the build: the next build rewrites the
`# nros-managed` row in each `Cargo.toml` to the generated `tutorial_msgs`
crate. A C or C++ build finds message packages with `find_package`, so
change that line in each node's `CMakeLists.txt` too:

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

Nothing more to change: `Cargo.toml` follows `package.xml`.

#### C

```bash probe=535 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)#find_package(tutorial_msgs REQUIRED)#' \
    src/sensor_node/CMakeLists.txt src/monitor_node/CMakeLists.txt
```

#### C++

```bash probe=535 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)#find_package(tutorial_msgs REQUIRED)#; s#std_msgs__nano_ros_cpp#tutorial_msgs__nano_ros_cpp#' \
    src/sensor_node/CMakeLists.txt src/monitor_node/CMakeLists.txt
```

The C++ node also links the generated C++ message library by name, which the
second substitution changes.

<!-- /tabs -->

## Publish a reading

Replace the talker's code. It publishes a `Reading` on `/reading` once a
second, with a sequence number and a temperature that steps through ten
values:

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=540 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node/src/lib.rs <<'EOF'
//! `sensor_node`: publishes a `tutorial_msgs/Reading` on `/reading` once a second.

#![no_std]

use nros::{
    Callback, CallbackCtx, Component, DeclarativeNode, ExecutableNode, NodeContext, NodeOptions,
    NodeResult, TimerDuration,
};
use nros_log::{Logger, log_info};
use tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading;

static LOGGER: Logger = Logger::new("sensor_node");

pub struct Talker;

impl Component for Talker {
    const NAME: &'static str = "sensor_node";
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(1, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        nros_log::register_logger(&LOGGER);
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("sensor_node"))?;
        let pub_reading = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<Reading>("/reading")?;
        let _timer =
            node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
        node.callback_for_name("on_tick")
            .publishes_entity(&pub_reading)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Talker {
    /// The sequence number of the last reading published.
    type State = i32;
    const HAS_TICK: bool = false;

    fn init() -> Self::State {
        0
    }

    fn on_callback(state: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
        if callback.as_str() == "on_tick" {
            *state = state.wrapping_add(1);
            let msg = Reading {
                sequence: *state,
                temperature_mc: 21_000 + (*state % 10) * 100,
            };
            let _ = ctx.publish_to_topic::<Reading, 32>("/reading", &msg);
            log_info!(&LOGGER, "Publishing: reading {} ({} mC)", msg.sequence, msg.temperature_mc);
        }
    }
}

nros::node!(Talker);
EOF
```

`tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading` is a plain Rust struct with one field per line
of the `.msg` file, generated under `generated/tutorial_msgs`. The `32` in
`publish_to_topic::<Reading, 32>` is the size of the buffer the message is
serialized into, in bytes; a `Reading` needs 12.

#### C

```bash probe=540 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node/src/Talker.c <<'EOF'
// sensor_node: publishes a tutorial_msgs/Reading on /reading once a second.
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

#include <rcl/rcl.h>
#include <rclc/executor.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>

#include <tutorial_msgs/tutorial_msgs.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_publisher_t pub;
    rcl_timer_t timer;
    int32_t count;
} talker_t;

static void on_tick(rcl_timer_t* timer, int64_t last_call_time) {
    talker_t* self = RCLC_CONTAINER_OF(timer, talker_t, timer);
    (void)last_call_time;
    self->count++;
    tutorial_msgs__msg__Reading msg;
    memset(&msg, 0, sizeof msg);
    msg.sequence = self->count;
    msg.temperature_mc = 21000 + (self->count % 10) * 100;
    if (rcl_publish(&self->pub, &msg, NULL) == RCL_RET_OK) {
        printf("Publishing: reading %d (%d mC)\n", (int)msg.sequence, (int)msg.temperature_mc);
    }
}

static rcl_ret_t talker_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor, talker_t* self) {
    setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0);
    self->count = 0;
    self->pub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_publisher();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_publisher_init_default(
        &self->pub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(tutorial_msgs, msg, Reading), "/reading");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    self->timer = rcl_get_zero_initialized_timer();
    rc = rclc_timer_init_default(&self->timer, NULL, 1000000000ULL, on_tick);
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_timer(executor, &self->timer);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(talker_t, talker_configure)
EOF
```

The generated header, `<tutorial_msgs/tutorial_msgs.h>`, declares
`tutorial_msgs__msg__Reading` with rosidl's C names, and
`ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(tutorial_msgs, msg, Reading)` names its type
support, as in rclc.

#### C++

```bash probe=540 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node/include/sensor_node/Talker.hpp <<'EOF'
#pragma once

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

#include "tutorial_msgs.hpp"

namespace sensor_node {

class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<::tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int32_t count_ = 0;

    void on_tick();

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

} // namespace sensor_node
EOF
```

```bash probe=541 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node/src/Talker.cpp <<'EOF'
#include "sensor_node/Talker.hpp"

#include <cstdio>

namespace sensor_node {

void Talker::on_tick() {
    ++count_;
    ::tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading msg;
    msg.sequence = count_;
    msg.temperature_mc = 21000 + (count_ % 10) * 100;
    if (pub_.publish(msg).ok()) {
        std::printf("Publishing: reading %d (%d mC)\n", static_cast<int>(msg.sequence),
                    static_cast<int>(msg.temperature_mc));
    }
}

::rclcpp::Result Talker::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::setvbuf(stdout, nullptr, _IOLBF, 0);
    ::rclcpp::Result r = node.create_publisher(pub_, "/reading");
    if (!r.ok()) return r;
    return node.create_wall_timer<Talker, &Talker::on_tick>(timer_, 1000, this);
}

} // namespace sensor_node
EOF
```

The generated header, `tutorial_msgs.hpp`, declares
`tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading` with the member names of the `.msg` file, as
rclcpp's generated headers do.

## Hear a reading

Replace the listener's code to match. It subscribes to `/reading` and
prints both fields:

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```bash probe=545 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/monitor_node/src/lib.rs <<'EOF'
//! `monitor_node`: subscribes to `/reading` and logs each reading.

#![no_std]

use nros::{
    Callback, CallbackCtx, Component, DeclarativeNode, ExecutableNode, NodeContext, NodeOptions,
    NodeResult,
};
use nros_log::{Logger, log_info};
use tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading;

static LOGGER: Logger = Logger::new("monitor_node");

pub struct Listener;

impl Component for Listener {
    const NAME: &'static str = "monitor_node";
    const ENTITY_BOUNDS: nros::EntityBounds = nros::EntityBounds::exact(0, 0, 0, 0, 0);

    fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
        nros_log::register_logger(&LOGGER);
        let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("monitor_node"))?;
        let _sub =
            node.create_subscription_for_callback_name::<Reading>("on_reading", "/reading")?;
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl ExecutableNode for Listener {
    /// Number of readings seen.
    type State = i32;
    const HAS_TICK: bool = false;

    fn init() -> Self::State {
        0
    }

    fn on_callback(state: &mut Self::State, callback: Callback<'_>, ctx: &mut CallbackCtx<'_>) {
        if callback.as_str() == "on_reading"
            && let Ok(msg) = ctx.message::<Reading>()
        {
            *state = state.wrapping_add(1);
            log_info!(&LOGGER, "I heard: reading {} ({} mC)", msg.sequence, msg.temperature_mc);
        }
    }
}

nros::node!(Listener);
EOF
```

#### C

```bash probe=545 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/monitor_node/src/Listener.c <<'EOF'
// monitor_node: subscribes to /reading and prints each reading.
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdio.h>

#include <rcl/rcl.h>
#include <rclc/executor.h>
#include <rclc/rclc.h>

#include <tutorial_msgs/tutorial_msgs.h>

typedef struct {
    rcl_subscription_t sub;
    tutorial_msgs__msg__Reading msg;
    int recv;
} listener_t;

static void on_msg(const void* msgin, void* ctx) {
    listener_t* self = (listener_t*)ctx;
    const tutorial_msgs__msg__Reading* msg = (const tutorial_msgs__msg__Reading*)msgin;
    printf("I heard: reading %d (%d mC)\n", (int)msg->sequence, (int)msg->temperature_mc);
    self->recv++;
}

static rcl_ret_t listener_configure(rcl_node_t* node, rclc_executor_t* executor, listener_t* self) {
    setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IOLBF, 0);
    self->recv = 0;
    self->sub = rcl_get_zero_initialized_subscription();
    rcl_ret_t rc = rclc_subscription_init_default(
        &self->sub, node, ROSIDL_GET_MSG_TYPE_SUPPORT(tutorial_msgs, msg, Reading), "/reading");
    if (rc != RCL_RET_OK) {
        return rc;
    }
    return rclc_executor_add_subscription_with_context(executor, &self->sub, &self->msg, on_msg,
                                                       self, ON_NEW_DATA);
}

RCLC_C_COMPONENT(listener_t, listener_configure)
EOF
```

The message lives in the node's state struct, so nothing allocates when a
reading arrives. A `Reading` holds no string or sequence, so it needs no
storage beyond the struct.

#### C++

```bash probe=545 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/monitor_node/include/monitor_node/Listener.hpp <<'EOF'
#pragma once

#include <rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp>

#include "tutorial_msgs.hpp"

namespace monitor_node {

class Listener {
    int recv_ = 0;

    void on_reading(const ::tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading& msg);

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};

} // namespace monitor_node
EOF
```

```bash probe=546 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/monitor_node/src/Listener.cpp <<'EOF'
#include "monitor_node/Listener.hpp"

#include <cstdio>

namespace monitor_node {

void Listener::on_reading(const ::tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading& msg) {
    std::printf("I heard: reading %d (%d mC)\n", static_cast<int>(msg.sequence),
                static_cast<int>(msg.temperature_mc));
    ++recv_;
}

::rclcpp::Result Listener::configure(::rclcpp::Node& node) {
    ::setvbuf(stdout, nullptr, _IOLBF, 0);
    return ::rclcpp::bind_subscription<::tutorial_msgs::msg::Reading, Listener,
                                       &Listener::on_reading>(node, "/reading", this);
}

} // namespace monitor_node
EOF
```

## Run it

```bash probe=550 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run --expect 'I heard: reading'
```

```text probe-expect=550 variant=qemu
I heard: reading 1 (21100 mC)
nros run: matched after
```

The first lines of the build show the new package being generated before
anything compiles (a Rust project's output, trimmed):

```text
sync: codegen tutorial_msgs
sync: message dependencies → /home/you/sensor_ws/src/sensor_node/Cargo.toml
sync: message dependencies → /home/you/sensor_ws/src/monitor_node/Cargo.toml
```

and the console ends with the readings:

```text
[INFO] sensor_node: [    1.330477] Publishing: reading 1 (21100 mC)
[INFO] monitor_node: [    1.406537] I heard: reading 1 (21100 mC)
nros run: matched after 1.7 s: [INFO] monitor_node: [    1.406537] I heard: reading 1 (21100 mC)
```

A C or C++ project prints the same two lines without the `[INFO]` prefix.
`ls generated` now lists `tutorial_msgs` beside the packages generated
before it. A package no node depends on any more stays there until you delete
`generated/`; it is never linked into the image, so it costs nothing on the
board.

The topic changed with the type: both nodes now use `/reading`, and nothing
publishes on `/chatter` any more. A topic's name and its type travel
together, so a subscriber on `/reading` with another type would match
nothing, on the board or in ROS 2.

## Your own, or one from ROS 2

ROS 2 already ships a temperature message, `sensor_msgs/msg/Temperature`.
A node uses it exactly as it used `std_msgs`: `<depend>sensor_msgs</depend>`
in its `package.xml`, and the build generates it from your ROS 2 install. Use
an installed message when the machines you talk to expect it: a ROS 2 tool
that plots temperatures reads `sensor_msgs/msg/Temperature`, not yours.

Write your own when no standard message fits, or when the standard one costs
more than the board can spend. `Temperature` carries a `std_msgs/Header`,
whose `frame_id` is an unbounded string, and two `float64` fields, so every
sample needs a string capacity and floating-point formatting to print.
`Reading` is 8 bytes of payload. The choice is per message, and a workspace
can mix both: one node can depend on `tutorial_msgs` and `sensor_msgs` at
once. Whichever you pick, a peer that receives it needs the same definition:
for a ROS 2 machine, an installed package or the same `.msg` source built
there.

## Change it

Add a field and follow it through. Append a line to `Reading.msg`:

```text
int32 humidity_pct    # relative humidity, percent
```

then set `humidity_pct` in the talker and print it in the listener. The next
`nros run` regenerates `tutorial_msgs` before it compiles anything, and a node
that sets or reads a field the message lacks fails to compile, naming the
field. Nothing else in the workspace needs to know the message changed: the
two nodes share it through `package.xml`, never through each other.

## If it doesn't work

- **`nros interface show` says the type is not found:** the package is not
  where the search starts. It must sit directly under `src/`, with its
  `package.xml` and a `msg/` directory beside it.
- **Rust: `unresolved import tutorial_msgs`:** the node's `package.xml` still
  depends on `std_msgs` only. Check the `<depend>` line, then run again; the
  build writes the `Cargo.toml` row.
- **C or C++: CMake cannot find `tutorial_msgs`:** the node's
  `CMakeLists.txt` still says `find_package(std_msgs REQUIRED)`. Change it,
  and for C++ the `target_link_libraries` line too.
- **The build stops naming `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`:** the generator reads
  `rosidl_default_generators` and the base types from ROS 2. Source ROS 2 in
  this shell, as in chapter 1.

## What just happened

You wrote a **message package**, and the build turned it into code for every
node that depends on it.

A message package holds definitions and no code. Its `msg/` directory is the
whole interface; `package.xml` names it and marks it an interface package
with `<member_of_group>rosidl_interface_packages</member_of_group>`. On each
build, `nros` finds every message package a node depends on, in this order,
and generates code for it under `generated/`:

1. a package under the workspace's `src/`, such as `tutorial_msgs`;
2. a package in your ROS 2 install, such as `std_msgs`, through
   `AMENT_PREFIX_PATH` or the prefix the workspace's first build recorded;
3. a few standard packages the nano-ros release carries, which only fill
   gaps under a ROS 2 install and never stand in for one.

A workspace package shadows an installed one of the same name, whole: it
replaces all of that package's messages, not one of them.

What the build generates is where nano-ros differs from ROS 2. ROS 2
generates code that allocates: a `std::string`, a `std::vector`, rosidl's
`__init` and `__fini` in C. nano-ros generates code for a board with no heap.
A Rust message is a `no_std` struct built on fixed-capacity types. A C
message's strings and sequences point at memory the node owns. Because
nothing grows at run time, an unbounded `string` or `[]` sequence in a
`.msg` file needs a capacity stated at build time. A C or C++ node states it
in `nros-codegen.toml` beside its `package.xml`: the scaffold wrote one for
`std_msgs/String`, `"std_msgs/String.data" = 256`. `Reading` holds two
integers, so it needs none.

On the wire nothing differs. The generated types serialize to the same CDR
bytes and carry the same type name, `tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading`, as the code
ROS 2 generates from the same `.msg` file. That is why chapter 10 can build
the same package with `colcon` and hear the board with `ros2 topic echo`.
[Message generation](../reference/message-generation.md) lists what the
build generates and the CMake functions behind it.

## Design background

Generating message code from the stock ROS 2 package shape, with the
workspace first on the search path, follows
[RFC-0094](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0094-resolve-before-configure.md)
and
[RFC-0098](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0098-generated-leaf-build-config.md).
